video_title: AI in NYC: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native Engineering Team — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
gist: Tenex co-founder Alex Lieberman and special projects lead CJ Hess describe running a 75-person AI-native services firm that pays engineers by story points (output roughly 2x this year on Opus 5.5) and map enterprise AI adoption: 90% have an LLM rolled out but only ~5% have non-engineering agents in production. They debate vertical AI and SaaS durability, arguing big systems of record like Salesforce/SAP are safe while vertical AI apps face margin pressure.

insights.claim: Tenex, an applied AI partner helping enterprises go from 'AI absent to AI native', has grown to 75 people in 18 months, with 90% of staff being engineers or AI strategists (technical consultants).
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: AI-transformation services is scaling fast as a category; watch for consultancy share shifts away from traditional firms.

insights.claim: Tenex's customer base is roughly 50% Fortune 2000 and 50% mid-market companies with $100-500M revenue, and demand shifted from staff-augmented AI engineering to 'AI transformation as a service'.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: Enterprise demand is for end-to-end AI transformation, not just engineering capacity — a services TAM that traditional consultancies compete for.
insights.quote: They were asking for like AI transformation as a service.

insights.claim: Tenex pays engineers by story points (output) rather than hours, and the spread between its highest- and lowest-paid engineers is about 4x, supporting the thesis that AI widens earnings dispersion.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: AI acts as leverage on individual talent; expect compensation models across software services to shift toward outcome-based pay.
insights.quote: AI is really just a leveraged bet on a human's intellect and work ethic. And so you're just going to have more variance than ever before in earning capacity.

insights.claim: Feared failure modes of output-based pay (sandbagged story points, low-quality code) have not materialized at Tenex because AI strategists are incentivized on customer retention and growth, counterbalancing engineers; the real problem is compensating non-coding time like architecting and client meetings.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: A template for services firms moving to outcome pricing: pair output-paid producers with retention-paid account owners.

insights.claim: As models get engineers to ~90% of a solution given the right context, the value of engineering work is shifting toward eliciting customer context, so Tenex expects to move from pure story-point pricing toward measuring the actual outcome delivered.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Billable-hours and even unit-of-work pricing in IT services is under pressure; outcome-based pricing likely spreads.
insights.quote: companies are gonna pay based on outcome and they're not going to want to pay based on the time that's required to build something

insights.claim: Tenex runs a 'meta harness': standardized skills, structured in-repo documentation and a CLI that agents use to create plans, visualizations, client readouts and decision logs, all checked into Git so context lives in the repo rather than people's heads.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Durable repo-resident context is becoming core infrastructure for long-running agent work; tooling around agent memory/docs is a growth area.

insights.claim: CJ Hess argues code alone is not sufficient memory for a codebase: agents need recorded rationale and conversation context for decisions, though Tenex has reduced enforced plan structure as models improved.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Less scaffolding needed as models improve, but decision-record tooling retains value.

insights.claim: Average engineer output at Tenex, measured as story points per engineer per month, roughly doubled (2x) over the past year, from the 'Opus 4.5 moment' in December to Opus 5.5.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of ~2x productivity gain from frontier coding models — supports demand for frontier model APIs and AI-native services margins.

insights.claim: Tenex recalibrates story-point criteria at least quarterly because, as models improve, a story point should theoretically deflate in value.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Output-based pricing in an AI world requires ongoing unit deflation — watch for margin compression in services priced per unit of work.

insights.claim: At Tenex the default driver model is Anthropic's Opus 5.5, which CJ Hess says now covers the full range he previously split across two to three models because it is fast, cheap and smart; many are defaulting away from Fable.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Signals strong practitioner share for Anthropic's Opus line in coding; a single cheap frontier model reduces multi-model routing demand.
insights.quote: Opus is so good. It's fast, it's cheap. It kind of hits all my checkboxes.

insights.claim: Tenex's best-practice workflow pairs Opus 5.5 as the driver with OpenAI's Codex as a reviewer working back and forth, with Codex also preferred for computer-use tasks.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Cross-model review is a durable pattern; multi-vendor usage limits lock-in for any one lab.

insights.claim: CJ Hess prefers Amp's opinionated cloud 'orbs' over Claude Code in the cloud and Claude Tag for cross-model remote agent work, and Amp's ability to hook in a Claude Code subscription cuts costs by around 80%.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Opinionated third-party agent harnesses can beat lab-native products on remote environments; subscription bring-your-own pricing shifts economics.
insights.quote: Isn't it weird that Anthropic never captured the remote environment thing in the way that Orbs did?

insights.claim: Tenex's raw token spend runs at roughly 1:1 to 2:1 versus employee spend, which the host calls high relative to typical companies ($10-200 per employee) and the ~1x of an average AI startup employee.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Token budgets approaching or exceeding payroll at AI-native firms imply large, growing inference demand per knowledge worker.

insights.claim: Tenex's AI costs fell sharply after switching to Opus 5.5 from expensive models like Astra and Fable, ending the industry's 'token-maxing' era of leaderboards followed by cost shock.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Per-task inference costs are falling fast; spend shifts toward cheaper-but-sufficient frontier models, pressuring premium model pricing.

insights.claim: Alex Lieberman believes per-task AI costs have hit a Pareto point where it is far harder for a token-maxing employee to blow up company costs than it was six to eight months ago.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: AI budget risk for enterprises is declining, easing a key adoption objection.

insights.claim: CJ Hess argues most economically valuable tasks can already be done with Opus 5.5, so a 10x smarter but far more expensive model would rarely be justified; cheap frontier releases like Muse Wonder and open-source competition will keep driving costs down.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Diminishing returns to raw intelligence for everyday tasks implies price competition, not capability, dominates the mass market.
insights.quote: would a 10 times smarter model really justify the cost of moving some cells in a spreadsheet? Probably not.

insights.claim: Alex Lieberman is skeptical that AI data vendors like Micro One, Mercore and Handshake (90%+ of revenue from labs) can flip to enterprise-driven revenue, since that requires enterprises to fine-tune their own models when the frontier keeps moving and token prices keep falling.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: Bearish signal on AI-data-labeling vendors' enterprise diversification story; their revenue stays concentrated in labs.

insights.claim: Among ~100 enterprises Tenex talks to, 90% have rolled out a general-purpose LLM (Claude or Codex), ~60% have done training and enablement, only ~50% have meaningfully deployed coding agents to engineering/product, and only ~5% have agents in production for non-engineering work.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: The biggest diffusion gap is production agents outside engineering — the main growth runway for agent platforms and AI services firms.
insights.quote: agents in production for non-engineering work drops to like 5%.

insights.claim: The most common enterprise ask is building agents for repeatable back-office tasks, and the second is data permissioning/RBAC, which has become a 'nightmare' for CIOs and CISOs as every employee gets Claude or Codex; Tenex has productized its own AI gateway.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: AI gateways and data-permissioning control planes are an acute enterprise pain point and investable category.

insights.claim: CJ Hess says 'you can't automate a process that does not exist': when 40 people do the same function differently, organizations must standardize the process first before agents and evals can be built.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Agent deployment timelines are gated by process standardization, implying slower-than-hyped enterprise rollout and services demand for process redesign.
insights.quote: you can't automate a process that does not exist.

insights.claim: Tenex is generally bearish on vertical-specific AI solutions (e.g., Harvey for law, OpenEvidence for medicine) because buyers now expect one-of-one software, forcing FDE-heavy services that threaten software margins, and frontier models may absorb them.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: Questions software-like margins for vertical AI apps as services and software converge.
insights.quote: how will they be able to do this at software margins if everyone expects a one-of-one solution?

insights.claim: The host pushes back that vertical AI winners like Harvey and Legora have moats in proprietary data, focus and domain-specific UI affordances (e.g., Harvey's Tabular Review), akin to why traders pay ~$50,000/year for Bloomberg despite free exchange data.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Counterpoint: workflow lock-in and specialized affordances can sustain vertical AI pricing power.

insights.claim: The host expects a small set of companies to own the agent interface with others plugging in data via APIs/MCP, noting Salesforce is embracing this by offering APIs and MCPs rather than pushing its own agents.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Interface consolidation favors horizontal agent owners; systems of record may monetize via data access rather than agent seats.

insights.claim: Alex Lieberman disagrees that Salesforce and SAP are at risk from AI rebuilds, arguing large systems of record accrue value because ripping them out risks hundreds of millions or billions of dollars.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: Supports holding large enterprise systems-of-record against 'death of SaaS' narratives; risk concentrates in mid-tier SaaS.
insights.quote: Salesforce is really at risk. SAP is really at risk. Like don't agree with that at all.

insights.claim: The host replaced a mid-tier SaaS quoted at $40,000/year with a ~$1,000 in-house build; Lieberman frames the build-vs-buy decision as whether the prize justifies the cognitive load of maintaining non-core software, which favors nimble startups over entrenched enterprises.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Mid-tier SaaS faces churn from smaller, nimble customers, but enterprise churn is less likely; watch SMB-heavy SaaS names.

insights.claim: CJ Hess argues AI will displace functions like call centers but Tenex focuses agent deployments on reallocating staff to next-priority problems, with Alex Lieberman adding that workers must take agency to assess their own job's replaceability and reskill.
insights.speaker: CJ Hess
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI adoption may be framed as reallocation rather than headcount cuts, moderating near-term labor savings.

insights.claim: Alex Lieberman sees New York as a smaller AI pond than San Francisco but as big or bigger for commercial value, creating an arbitrage of bringing SF builders to NYC customers for diffusion with meaningful GDP impact.
insights.speaker: Alex Lieberman
insights.so_what: NYC enterprise density makes it a key market for AI services and diffusion-focused firms.
insights.quote: we're in a smaller pond for AI but I would argue we're in as big of a pond if not a bigger pond for like commercial value
